title: FPRAS for #BIS
formal: Does there exist one probabilistic Turing algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every finite simple bipartite graph G and rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1), A(G,\varepsilon )\) halts within \(p(\mathrm{L},\lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil )\) steps on every random tape and returns a nonnegative rational Ẑ with \(\Pr [(1- \varepsilon )Z(G)\le \hat\{Z\}\le (1+\varepsilon )Z(G)]\ge 3/4\)? L is the full input bit length, including \(\varepsilon ; Z(G)\) is the number of independent sets.
definitions: The input lists the vertices, their bipartition U,V and all edges, with no loops or repeated edges; \(\varepsilon\) is supplied as a positive binary numerator and denominator. An independent set \(I\subseteq U\cup V\) contains no edge’s two endpoints. \(Z(G)\) counts all such subsets, including \(\varnothing\), so \(Z(G)\ge 1\) and the empty graph has \(Z=1\). The output is a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator representing \(\hat\{Z\}\ge 0\). A uses independent fair coin bits, with no advice or oracle. All input reading, computation, random-bit access and output writing count toward the bound. The success probability is separately required on every input and is over A’s coins. The same program and polynomial work for all bipartitions, degrees, graph sizes and accuracies.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: Determines whether the canonical intermediate approximate-counting problem can be solved with a uniform polynomial-time randomized relative-error algorithm, with consequences for many equivalent counting and statistical-mechanics problems.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting, with broad approximation-preserving consequences and a well-defined gap between FPRAS and hardness evidence.

progress.text: Dell, Husfeldt and Nederlof describe #BIS as the canonical approximate-counting problem of intermediate complexity and record the belief that it has no efficient approximation algorithm without being NP-hard.
Liao, Lin, Lu and Mao give an FPTAS for independent sets on almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph, a restricted result that leaves arbitrary worst-case graphs open.
Container and spectral methods give FPRAS or FPTAS results for additional dense, regular, or expanding subclasses, without resolving general #BIS.

status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No FPRAS for #BIS on arbitrary bipartite graphs, and no unconditional impossibility theorem, was found in the cited literature; the positive results listed here impose structural restrictions.
review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial; restricted-family approximation results do not settle the unrestricted target.

context_blocks.text: #BIS asks for the number of independent sets in an arbitrary bipartite graph. Exact counting is already difficult, while approximate counting places the problem in a widely studied intermediate regime: it is a canonical complete problem for the class #\(RH\Pi _{1}\) under approximation-preserving reductions, and many spin-system and combinatorial counting problems are equivalent to it. The main unresolved issue is whether this intermediate status hides a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme.

The relative-error requirement matters when the graph has few independent sets as well as when it has exponentially many. The algorithm must work for every explicitly encoded graph and every requested accuracy, with no structural promise that would make local sampling mix rapidly. A polynomial bound in |V| alone, an additive approximation, or an algorithm whose polynomial degree depends on the graph family would be a different statement.

Several restricted classes do admit efficient approximation schemes. For example, results for almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph and for dense regular bipartite graphs exploit expansion or spectral structure. These theorems demonstrate that the target is achievable on substantial subclasses, but they do not provide a worst-case FPRAS for arbitrary bipartite inputs.

The conjectured difficulty is deliberately weaker than #P-hardness of approximation. #BIS is believed not to have an FPRAS, yet it is also believed not to be NP-hard under the usual approximation-preserving reductions. Resolving the card would therefore locate a central intermediate point between problems with known FPRASes and problems with robust hardness barriers.

The earlier catalogue pointer TCS-6225 came from a paper on independent sets in random regular bipartite graphs and preserved only a truncated source excerpt. This card states the general #BIS question explicitly and keeps the restricted-family results as progress rather than treating them as a solution.
